utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-95-14-R77.6, the Prosecutor versus Domagoj Margetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland, Salvatore Cannata, assisted by Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Veljko Miljevic, attorney-at-law from Zagreb, Defence counsel for the accused Domagoj Margetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljevic. Mr. Margetic, I had not yet asked you whether you can hear me and the others speaking in this courtroom in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear it, Your Honour, but I would just like to note that I haven't been feeling very well for several days now, so from the point of view of my health, I am really unwell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any medical report to support this, Mr. Miljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client, the accused Margetic, was not receiving any kind of medical treatment and was not sent to hospital, although an emergency team was supposed to send him to the Mercury hospital in Zagreb three days ago. However, due to these proceedings having being scheduled, he has refused that. Nevertheless, he has not been feeling well. Today he felt well enough to appear before the Court. So I believe that although the state of his health is very poor, and I think that is due to the very unfavourable climate at present in Zagreb, he is nonetheless in a position to following the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljevic. Mr. Margetic, if your health would deteriorate to such an extent that you'd consider that you could not follow these proceedings and not be able to instruct counsel, please address me and then the Chamber will consider that situation. Then, Ms. Sutherland, the Chamber has received a motion asking for two things. First of all, disclosure, and second, disclosure of documents, and second, to dismiss the case right away. I'd like to ask you to respond to that motion. I know that usually there's more time to respond to a motion, but it goes without saying that it doesn't make much sense to give you the usual time. So you're invited to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly in relation to the first matter of dismissing all the charges. It's the Prosecution's submission that there has been a case to answer. The Prosecution brought evidence last Thursday which, in our submission, fulfils the -- the elements of the charges and, therefore, there should be no dismissal of the case. That's it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the dismissal of the case. And about disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: About disclosure, Your Honour, in the Prosecution's view, there is no Rule 68 material to be disclosed. The witness list, in our submission, has always been a confidential document and still remains so. We -- there is no 11 July, 2006 decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other decision of that same one which might have some relevance for the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a decision earlier in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: However, that does not make the witness list a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I do understand that's your interpretation of the document, but the question is whether that document could have relevance. But it could, also in view of what the Defence took as it's -- as it's major argument, whether that could have any real relevance for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is the decision of the 3rd of July of the Trial Chamber admitting the witness list into the Jovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have that exhibit here, but we have not disclosed that because, in our view, that's not exculpatory material. We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there only a duty to disclose exculpatory material? Could you explain to us why, looking at the line of the defence, this could not, not saying what it finally would do, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has -- has a burden, obligation to disclose evidence that it's going to bring in its own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's under 66, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And under Rule 68, anything that may exculpate the accused. And in our view, this decision does not make the document a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And should it have been included in relevant material under 68(2), which is not exculpatory material, but -- relevant material held by the Prosecutor? So we could avoid a discussion on whether it's exculpatory or not. Would you consider this to be without relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Given the defence that's been raised last Thursday, that document could be seen as being relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have to make a ruling or are you willing to, based on what you said, that you feel that the Prosecution would be in an obligation to disclose this material as being relevant although not exculpatory under Rule 68(2)?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can provide a copy now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber invites you to disclose that document to the Prosecution -- to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we have dealt with that matter, there is one matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps let's do -- if you want to bring something to our attention, please do so, and then once you have done so, Mr. Miljevic, then I'd like to hear from you whether you'd need more time to review this document just disclosed to you and considered to be relevant, or whether we could proceed. Yes. Then, Ms. Sutherland, you may address us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we adjourned last Thursday, Your Honour sought a commitment from the accused that he would not publish anything in relation to this case, and the accused gave an unequivocal undertaking, and he said, "Your Honour, Mr. President, I undertake not to discuss the proceedings in any way, and you can see that I have not published anything about the Tribunal or the proceedings in my blog, and I have absolutely no intention of discussing the proceedings with anyone. I will comply fully with the order that I have already received from you, Your Honour." I'd like to provide the Chamber with a document, and if that could be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it has been disclosed to Mr. Miljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, so the Chamber receives a document now which you are aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether you want to deal with this matter now or at the close of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- what would be your preference?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One doesn't normally deal with contempt within a contempt proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Contempt within a contempt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I -- I leave it in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'd like to hear from Mr. Miljevic what he thinks is the proper conduct of the proceedings in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what document you're referring to. If it's the document that I received just now, dated the 3rd of July, 2006, then the Defence -- oh, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now talking about the other document, that is the document the Prosecution would like to tender. It has got something to do, I take it, with publication on the Internet of events related to this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was on the website margetic.blog.hr, and it appeared on -- at least on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of December and possibly before that date as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, we are talking about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I got that document about 10 minutes ago. I managed to look at the content of the document. It's quite clear to me everything that's written here. However, I cannot state anything in relation to the content of the document. I've seen it, and my client can state his views on it, the accused Margetic. I have nothing to state. Otherwise, I believe that is not the subject of these proceedings. Perhaps it can be the subject of some other proceedings, but most certainly not these proceedings in relation to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miljevic, the Chamber has some difficulty in accepting your last -- that it can not be subject of some other proceedings but most certainly not these proceedings. It is about a commitment made in the framework of these proceedings. At the same time, I notice that Mr. Margetic would like to say something. Is that true, Mr. Margetic? And, if so, please tell us what you would like to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I adhered to all instructions issued by this Tribunal, even more so, as I've been ill. So I haven't been doing any writing on my web page. As for what we received from the Prosecution, thank God everyone can see that I did not write that, but Brian Gallagher, a British journalist. Indeed, Your Honours, I have fully abided by your order. I wish to note to you that it says here in the text, when journalist called me and asked me to make a statement, Your Honours, I said that I have been instructed to the effect that proceedings are confidential and that I am not allowed to discuss it. And you see, Your Honours, that the British journalist, in his text, quoted me accurately. It's not my fault if some journalist looked something up on the Internet and is now writing about that. I really cannot be held responsible for other journalists' articles. Then I can be prosecuted for the articles written by all journalists who write about this Tribunal. I'm not the author of these texts and that can be seen very clearly. I was sick in bed for the last 10 days or a week, and I should have been in hospital, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it contested that this was published on the website http://margetic.blog.hr/?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, over the past 10 days several web pages appeared where they write about my case. The right address of my blog is www.margetic.com. So that is not the right address. This is a blog that was opened by way of support to me and people published some of my articles about domestic policies in Croatia. However, I have nothing whatsoever to do with these articles. I did not write them. I did not publish them, Your Honours. I have fully abided by your order. That can easily be checked. I didn't want to give any statements to Vecernji list, Hrvatski list, HINA, no media. I told everyone that I was not allowed to make any statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, your position is clear. Mr. Miljevic, could you tell us whether you need more time to look at the material that was just disclosed to you, that is the 3rd of July decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes at the most, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until 25 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, have you had an opportunity to look at the newly disclosed material? So I'm not talking about the web blogs, but about the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have now had an opportunity to read this material dated the 3rd of July this year, and I think that in terms of Rule 68(2), it is relevant material. However, as for our own motion that was sent in the English language from Zagreb yesterday on the 7th of December, 2006, it is evident that the decision of the Chamber, presided over by Judge Robinson on the 22nd of August this year, it is clear that this decision was based on a Prosecution motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are arguing now your case. My question simply was whether you had seen it because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- my next question -- the 3rd of July you said I have now had an opportunity to read this material. So the answer seems to be yes. And then my next question would be whether we could proceed with the case or whether you would need more time to study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now managed to read this document dated the 3rd of July. It is relevant. However, we believe that exculpatory material is actually the Prosecution motion of the 21st of August upon which the decision of the Chamber of Judge Robinson was based on the 22nd of August. However, I would like to have more time with my client, who availed himself of this, of the opportunity of this break to study this other material that has to do with the publication of these articles by journalist Gallagher. So now he looked at these articles and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, the Chamber, of course, has used its time also to consider the other matter and we're not going to pursue that at this moment during this case. The Chamber understands why the Prosecution introduced it. Whether there should be a contempt in this contempt case is to be considered not now but at a later stage. Do I understand that you'd like to see the motion underlying the decision by Judge Robinson on the 22nd of August? Is that correctly understood, Mr. Miljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution motion dated the 21st of August, 2006, requesting a decision to be made, and the decision of the 22nd of August actually accepted that motion. The Prosecution motion is partly quoted in the decision of the 22nd of August, and that is why we would like the Prosecutor to disclose their motion dated the 21st of August in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our view, the motion is irrelevant. The decision is -- says what it says, and the decision again on the 22nd of August does not state that the witness list is a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say that it's irrelevant, if the 3rd of July decision is relevant, if the 22nd of August decision is relevant, it's not easy to understand that the motion underlying the 22nd of August decision would be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Irrelevant was a bad choice of words. It relates to obviously the 22nd of August decision. It was filed on a confidential basis in that case. The Trial Chamber chose to quote from part of the decision -- part of the motion. In our submission, the Defence doesn't need the motion. The decision stands on itself, and it in no way makes the witness list a public document. And if Your Honour wants me to expand more fully on why I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it then you would like to go into private session or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can make the submissions in -- in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, you're invited to make further submissions on the relevance of that material or irrelevance in the view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution position has always been that the witness list is confidential. The OTP's letter dated the 6th of April, 2006, which is Exhibit 3 in this case, addressed to Jovic and to this accused, explicitly warned them that the material was subject to oral and written non-disclosure orders. On the 26th of June, 2006, the Prosecution sought to have the witness list admitted into evidence in the Jovic case. The witness list was referenced in the annex to the motion as Exhibit C1 in the Marijacic and Rebic case. The Trial Chamber in the Marijacic and Rebic case deemed it relevant to that case, and the Prosecution deemed, therefore, that it was relevant in the Jovic case. The Chamber in the Marijacic and Rebic case admitted the document as a confidential document, and that's at transcript page, of the 19th of January, 2006, 284 to 285. On the 3rd of July, the Jovic Trial Chamber admitted the documents listed in annex 1, tables A and B into evidence and ordered the Registry to give appropriate exhibit numbers to the items of evidence. Nowhere in the decision does it state that Exhibit 18 is a public document. On the 22nd of August, the Jovic Trial Chamber issued a decision which ordered the Registrar to separate the confidential and public lists of the witness list which were contained in Exhibit 18 and to designate Exhibit 19 to the two confidential lists. Nowhere in the decision does it state that Exhibit 18 is or was a public document or that it was not confidential prior to the decision. The Prosecution cannot, of its own volition, change the status of a confidential document. It must first obtain permission to do so by a Chamber of the Tribunal. The witness list is a confidential document. It was filed as a confidential document in the Marijacic and Rebic case and that status remained in the Jovic case. The Defence assert that the documentary evidence, which shows that the exhibit was public, should have been disclosed pursuant to Rule 68, but it's the Prosecution position that the exhibit was never a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand all of that. Nevertheless, let's just -- for argument's sake, let me just imagine that in the motion preceding the 22nd of August decision, the Prosecution would say, "We made a huge mistake. We let something go into the public domain where we should not have done that. Please correct that by this and this." If that would be true, that certainly would be relevant for the Defence, wouldn't it? I mean, it's clear that you said that the decision doesn't say it ever was a public document, but if, for example, the Prosecution would have said so in its motion, which Mr. Miljevic doesn't know, he would like to have a look at it, that might be used by the Defence as supporting their position. So, therefore, your whole explanation doesn't come to the core of the problem. The core of the problem is whether the motion underlying the 22nd of August decision, whether that document could in any way assist the Defence any further than the decision of the 22nd of August does. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm just trying to locate a copy of it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland, have you located a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's just been brought up on the screen on the JDB. If I can just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can provide the Defence with a copy of the confidential -- confidentially filed motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can -- but again, it's our position that that motion does not assist the Defence, because the status of the document is given to it by the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecution cannot change the status of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand all that, but perhaps the Chamber would be assisted by having a full oversight of what happened in relation to public, non-public, et cetera. Therefore, I think it's certainly relevant. Whether it assists the Defence or not. It might even assist the Prosecution, which I would -- I don't think that you would say that it would not be relevant for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, then, disclosure will take place confidentially. Yes, you'll understand. And I hope Mr. Margetic also understands. Then, Ms. Sutherland, another question. We -- you had not put all your questions in cross-examination as you would like to put them to Mr. Margetic. Is any of these questions related to the motion, the motion of the 21st of August? If not, I'd like to give you an opportunity to proceed with your cross-examination of Mr. Margetic. And meanwhile, Mr. Miljevic can have a look at the 21st of August motion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you'll receive that, I take it, soon. Copies are prepared at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it's coming down in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miljevic, you will receive a copy of the 21st of August motion in a few moments. Meanwhile, I would like you to ask you, Mr. Margetic, to take the stand again to be further cross-examined. So would you please take the seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the accused Margetic will be cross-examined. He's ready, but he begs you just to give him five minutes because he needs to go to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is someone available to indicate to Mr. Margetic whether -- perhaps the security could assist Mr. Margetic in finding the bathroom, and then we'd really like to continue and not spend any more time on things that perhaps should have been done before. Mr. Margetic, would you please take the -- take the place where witnesses are examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic -- I would like Mr. Margetic to renew the solemn declaration he gave last time. Would you please read the solemn declaration, Mr. Margetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Margetic. You may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, it's your position that the witness list is a public document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not since the 22nd of August, but I did think it to be that between the 11th of July and the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that you say you saw on the Internet in mid-July which said that the document was now public, what did the document actually say?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now, but I do know that even after that other documents that I saw, the decision dated the 22nd of August and the press briefing of the 23rd of August, reassured me that I was right because these documents state quite clearly that those lists were made public, yet they should have been kept confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I asked you what was the content of the document that you saw on the Internet in the mid-July which told you that the document was -- that the witness list was public? What was -- what was the contents of that document? I'm not talking about the 22nd or the 23rd of August. I'm talking about the document that you said you saw on the Internet. Just tell the Court about the contents of that document.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I do remember that the document I saw on the Internet contained reference to public document number -- public Exhibit number 18, and that it in turn contained two witness lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did this document list all of the witnesses and say that a variation of protective measures had been lifted in relation to all the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all witnesses were listed there, but, for instance, when Stjepan Mesic was no longer a protected witness, the contents of his testimony was not published, but the fact of his testimony became public. And I had no reason to believe that anything else applied in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, I'm talking about the document that you say you saw on the Internet making this document, the witness list, public. Did it list all the witness names and say that a variation of protective measures had been granted in relation to all of those witnesses? Yes or no? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the witness list was not contained there, but it said public Exhibit number 18 for three witness lists. So I'm just telling you what I remember from the Internet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A moment ago you said two witness lists. What is it, two or three witness lists?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said three, and then the decision of the 22nd of August separated two lists. Two lists were set aside, but the original number of lists was three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the document that you saw in mid-July spoke about -- or mentioned Exhibit 18. Expressly said Exhibit 18 in the Jovic case is now a public document. Is that correct? Do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that is what happened. And the decisions that followed reassured me that I had been right, because the decisions that were published later speak about public Exhibit number 18 that was made public but should have been kept confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, that's your interpretation of that document. I don't agree with it. I will move on. You make no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. The document that you saw on the Internet, was that a document in the format of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember now, but I think that the -- the link was from a Tribunal server. You have to bear in mind that this was before my arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the link. I'm asking about the document itself. Was that a document that had the appearance of originating from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about opinions. I'm asking about facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appeared to be to me. So to me it looked like a document originating from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did it contain the word "public".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it mentioned public Exhibit number 18. I remember that clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, you make no mention of the fact that this witness list was made public in the accompanying article to the witness list that you published on www.domagojmargetic.com, do you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my previous testimony that we journalists, when we publish a document that used to be confidential, because of the exclusive nature of the information, we always put confidential document. That's what we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how we deal with any document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You don't have to give an explanation. I know what you testified to last time. It was a simple question. Did you or did you not put the fact that this witness list was -- had been made public in your accompanying article?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not consider that to be relevant for the article that I actually wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You made no mention of this in the second or third articles, did you, that you published?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this -- this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it's not irrelevant, Mr. Margetic, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic. Mr. Margetic. Whether a question is relevant or not is a matter to be argued later whether counsel -- it is not to be judged upon by a witness. Please proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, what you in fact did say in Exhibit 6, which is the first article, was, "I decided to publish this list of protected witnesses." And further down, "I am not bound by any obligation to protect a secret, anyone's and on anything. I'm not a secret agent, and my duty is not to hide confidential information. My duty, when I come into possession of such information, is to make it public, accessible to everyone." So you put there in that article that you were publishing protected witnesses, that it wasn't your duty to hide confidential information, and yet it's your position that this witness list was a public document.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part that you just quoted, I spoke about the principle that govern journalism, the principles that guide journalists when they write their texts and when they do their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, Exhibit 10, the second article, what you said in that article was, "Who were The Hague's protected witnesses." Exhibit 11, the second article, "I was sent the list of all the protected witnesses in the proceedings against Tihomir Blaskic." In Exhibit 23, on the 20th of August, 2006, in the handwritten note that you gave, "I give you my word and promise that I will never again disclose or in any way use confidential ICTY information." Why was there a need to refer constantly to protected witnesses and confidential information if in fact what you're saying is true, that the list was public?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You quoted the title of my article, which reads: "Who were the protected witnesses in The Hague." So this is in past tense. And this indicates quite clearly that they are no longer protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, the reason --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is a grammatical difference between English and Croatian here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The reason why the title is "Who were The Hague's protected witnesses" is because the Blaskic trial was back in 1997 and 1998. It's past tense. You were saying who were the protected witnesses in that case.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the Croatian language, the wording "who were the protected witnesses," this tense is used for when this no longer applies. This is the past tense in Croatian. So this is what I wrote, who were. At that time, I consider them not to be protected witnesses any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, if I say, who were the football players of Dinamo Zagreb, then you could think of who were football players. Are they still football players or are they not football players anymore or are they still playing for Dinamo Zagreb? This linguistic explanation is of no assistance to the Chamber. And I would say you focussed on one title. Could you also respond also to the other ones, that is, I will never again, at least that's what was put to you, I'll never disclose or in any way use -- I'll never again will disclose or in any way use confidential ICTY information. Could you respond to that as well, because such a linguistical way out seems not to be there or is that a wrong understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this statement -- well, I promise I would know longer publish confidential information of the International Criminal Tribunal. That statement I wrote to the International Criminal Tribunal from detention in Zagreb because I really wanted to make this promise. Once I found out that obviously the list became protected again after I heard of The Hague order. I wanted through this promise to have the Tribunal know that I would no longer wish to publish any kind of confidential information or to commit any violation vis-a-vis this Tribunal. However, before that, I did not know that this was confidential material. As soon as I found out, I removed the confidential material from my web page, and I never published it again. As for the promise, I sent it because it was only logical to me that I make this promise, that I give this undertaking to the Tribunal, that I would no longer publish confidential information once I found out that that was the nature of the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, in your first -- the second article that you wrote, which was entitled, "Who were The Hague Prosecution's protected witnesses," you state in that article: "It so transpired that the list of protected witnesses who testified against Tihomir Blaskic includes men whose first and last names are definitely not among the usual Bosniak Muslim ones in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the persons in question are those who have dubiously acquired Bosnia and Herzegovina citizenship." And then you go on to list a number of witnesses with their initials and their pseudonyms. You also said further in the article: "Isn't Carla Del Ponte therefore protecting international Islamic terrorists?" You provided the public audience with the identities of persons whom you describe as international Islamic terrorists, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how I described them. It is some international documents declaring them wanted persons say that, and also some international organisations represent in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have to realise that 11.000 terrorists are in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this point in time according to information of international agencies, not according to my own information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is how you described them in your article, did you not, the one that you published on your website, or on the website www.domagojmargetic.com?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned facts that are derived from documents of international organisations that have a presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your evidence on Thursday at page 138 that four of the witnesses were participants of various terrorist organisations. Even if this was true, and even accepting your scenario that the witness list was public, why publish the entire witness names, the entire list, if you didn't want to cause them any interference or harm?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, I published the list because I thought that it was a public document at the point in time when I published it. That was the primary reason why I published it. And then comparing information with the information of international organisations present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I came to the knowledge that I wrote about. But first and foremost, I published it because I thought that I was actually publishing a public document. Had I believed that -- I did not want to harm any witnesses, and that is proven by the fact that some witnesses -- I mean, you have the same names in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Several thousand people with the same names. I never published their addresses, their years of birth, no personal details that could identify them. As for identical names in Bosnia-Herzegovina like those from the witness list, there are 500 to 1.000 people of identical names. You can find that on the Internet. So there was no chance that anybody could have identified them. I did not publish their years of birth, their addresses, nothing that could disclose their identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, you published those names as witnesses who have testified in the Blaskic proceeding. You are narrowing down the names, are you not? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean narrowing down the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By publishing the names and saying that they testified in the Blaskic proceedings, you are narrowing down the names of people in order that they can be interfered with by you or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is quite untrue. I told you just now why that is impossible, because you have a witness's name and surname. As for people with such names and surnames, for example, there are about 500 persons with that same name and surname in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same name and surname. I did not publish anybody's address or year of birth, no personal details that would single out one out of those 500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, you're now testifying of what is possible and what is not possible, which is perhaps not -- it's logic rather than anything else. This is your logic. The Chamber will consider whether it has a similar logic. Ms. -- Ms. Sutherland, we are limited in our time. You've got a couple of more minutes but then we'll have to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, it's reasonably likely that, by coining the witnesses as international terrorists and publishing their identities, you would put them at risk of harm, would you not?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not identify them as terrorists. It was international agencies, international organisations present in Bosnia-Herzegovina that did that. Again, the High Representative's office from the European Union for Bosnia-Herzegovina and other agencies that are present in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, you've answered the question. I'll move on to another topic. You said in Exhibit 19, which is the memorandum of service of order to the Zagreb County Court, you told the Zagreb County Court that you removed the protected material from the website. You also say -- and that was on the 4th of August. You also say in Exhibit 20, which is the record of interrogation of you on the 6th of August at the Zagreb County Court, you told that court on that day that you again had removed the protected material from the website, and you testified last Thursday at page 136 that you also removed it. However, you didn't remove all the material relating to the protected witnesses, did you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was getting the material, I got the entire material, the entire list. I got it off my web page. I took it off my web page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You removed the witness list, but you kept the accompanying articles there which named protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally took off all the material that were related to the witnesses. Again, I'm saying it's not my fault if somebody else published something, but I took it off. In the report of the county court in Zagreb, the dates are not right, and I don't know why they became part of the report. On the 6th of August, in view of my hunger strike and my state of health, on that date I could barely say a few words in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, it's disingenuous of you to say that you removed the material when you didn't. You left the offending articles which named protected witnesses on your site. You simply removed the witness list. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm repeating what I did. I personally removed what you call the incriminating material from the website. And the website was abolished as such on the 1st of August, so there's no way that something could have appeared on the website on the 4th of August. The website no longer physically existed online from the 1st of August onwards. It was no longer on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know the evidence of Mr. Osorio which has been admitted by agreement with the Defence in this case, which is Exhibit 21, where Mr. Osorio states that he saw all of the material on the website www.domagojmargetic.com. The website was subsequently temporarily shutdown, and when it came back up, the offending articles were still there. Do you still say that you removed all the material?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 1st of August, I in no way returned my web page. That can easily be checked with the provider of Internet services, whether I did anything with my web page as from the 1st of August onwards. Madam Prosecutor, the provider of my Internet service can say exactly whether I did anything after the 1st of August. That would be quite untrue. If somebody else did something, I don't know about that, but I did not. The provider of Internet services can certainly confirm that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because an offline page was taken off the Internet on the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, turning to the other websites where this material, your material, is then reproduced onto other websites, and that's Exhibit 12 and Exhibit 13, which shows the articles on www.0011385.com on the 7th of August, the material is still there. And Exhibit 13 is the www.lijepanasadomovinahrvatska.com, which has hyperlinks back to your website and had the protected articles on that website. As a regular Internet user, you know that by putting material, by posting material onto a website, you have no control over its further dissemination when other web users can copy that material onto their own websites.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. There is a law on authorship rights. www.domagojmargetic.com was protected by copyright, and that was stated clearly at the bottom of the Internet page. According to Croatian law and international law, anybody who took any kind of information from that web page without my consent committed a violation without my express consent. You did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, I'm going to stop you there. The question was whether it's possible or not, not whether it is legal or not. Therefore, this type of interpretations does not exist with the Chamber at this moment. Ms. Sutherland, at the same time, I said you had a couple of minutes. These minutes are gone by now. You do not suggest that any of these later publications are any later than the 22nd of August, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So therefore it's mainly about what was on Mr. Margetic's mind that you asked him about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then -- I said a couple of minutes, and it's -- some eight minutes have gone. That's more than a couple.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One final last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Margetic, did -- did you provide consent to the other web users to put these articles onto their websites, in particular, Mr. Ivica Grgic?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, is there any need to put any further questions in redirect to Mr. Margetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the material that was disclosed to you today cause you to tender it in evidence, or would you like the Chamber to look at it, to consider it when making its determination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the question is -- because if you keep it for yourself, the Chamber will not be able to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask that the Trial Chamber look at this material. In the meantime, I've managed to read it, and I would particularly like to draw your attention to paragraphs 4 and 5 before the final proposal of the Prosecutor, and I believe that this is the most important document in this entire set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so, we first like to thank Mr. Margetic for his testimony in his own case and to invite him to go back to the place where the accused is seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. Which of these documents would you like to tender into evidence? Would you like to have the 3rd of July decision in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision of the 3rd of July may be relevant, but it is not a key document. But this motion of the 21st of August is definitely a key document, not just the relevant material but, in the Defence's view, this is definitely exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you tender that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, since you make the 22nd of August decision so pivotal to this case, isn't -- is my recollection right that it has not been tendered into evidence by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems to me that it was tendered into evidence last time, seven days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not from what I remember, but do I --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Registry has no record of Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Miljevic, I understand that at least it was your intention to have that in evidence, so if you tender it now, then there's a chance that it will be admitted. I see you're nodding yes. Is that -- have you got a copy for Madam Registrar so that at least we have a document, an exhibit in evidence, rather than just a reference to a document which is not in our hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that a record has been made of that in our transcript. The only copy of the 22nd of August decision that I had was handed over into the record. I don't know whether this was actually exhibited, but the transcript, I'm sure, will reveal that we actually handed it over and that it is now part of the record. When I examined the transcript, I made note of the fact that it was handed over or submitted, and now today we receive the 21st of August motion, and we would like to tender it into evidence. And I only have one copy of the 21st of August motion that has just been given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll receive another copy if you want to tender that in evidence at this moment. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can provide another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a clean copy, because I remember that it was an unclean copy the last time. Any objection against admission into evidence of the 3rd of July decision we are talking about? An exhibit number will be provided later by Madam Registrar. And then by the motion dated the 21st of August and the decision dated the 22nd of August all 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam registrar, the 3rd of July would have Exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1. And the 21st of August motion would have ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the 22nd of August would shall Defence 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Exhibit 2 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are all under seal. Certainly D1, D2, D3 as well all under seal. Yes. Mr. Miljevic, that means that these documents are not in the public domain. And, Mr. Margetic, that these documents, not saying whether they ever were, but at least from this moment, from now on are certainly not in the public domain, and you should keep that in mind very carefully. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a procedural matter for Exhibit 35 of the Prosecution exhibits. I don't think that was actually tendered into evidence last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which was the e-mail the 3rd of April from Sebastiaan van Hooydonk to Domagoj Margetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the letter accompanying the forwarded exhibit list. It's -- no. I'm now confusing matters. Yes. Are you talking about the -- did you say the 3rd of April or -- not the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was -- the e-mail sent on the 3rd of April attaching an electronic copy of the letter which was dated the 6th of August [sic] which was then provided to Mr. Margetic via courier which he received then on the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said it was Exhibit number 35. Yes. Yes. It has --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's on page 144 and 145 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said it wasn't actually tendered but now it is. I do understand. Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit number 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Miljevic? I see you're nodding no. Then Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection. First of all, there is no document dated 3rd of April. There is a document dated 6th of April that is now tendered into evidence, but this document dated the 6th of April, 2006, was never received by Domagoj Margetic. Furthermore, the Prosecutor obviously got her months mixed up, because it is impossible to send something in August for the accused to receive it on the 16th of May. So we have a complete case here. Domagoj Margetic said quite clearly, and there is a Prosecution document to that effect, that on the 15th of May he had received a CD, but the covering letter dated the 6th of April was not received by him. And as regards August, the month of August, this has absolutely nothing to do with this whole affair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that -- I don't know how it came onto the transcript, but I think that where on page 32, line 7, the word August appears that April was meant. Is that correct, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That having been clarified. Then there is a document on the 3rd of April, that is Exhibit 35, Mr. Miljevic, and that's an e-mail which preceded the 6th of April letter. That's how I understood it. Is that a correct understanding, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other objection, Mr. Miljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have more objections. The 3rd of April memo cannot have anything to do with the disclosure that was carried out in May. So the 3rd of April memo, as my defendant said, this he never received. I'm talking about facts. Domagoj Margetic never took receipt of anything in April, and as -- as regards the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about admission of evidence. We are not talking about evaluation of evidence. We're not talking about to what extent this evidence is contradicted by anyone else. Any objection against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Exhibit 35, Prosecution 35, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the last few remarks, the Bench would have one or more questions to Mr. Margetic, so I would like, Mr. Margetic, you to take the stand again and to listen carefully to the questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Domagoj Margetic will respond to all the questions from the Bench, but he would like to get a five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're running out of time. To the extent that Mr. Margetic could stand it for another 15 minutes, he's invited to do so. If it's really impossible, then of course we'll let him go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. He will bear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, Judge Moloto will have one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is on. Looking at Exhibit 6, which was the article accompanying your -- your publication of the list, you indicated that you received the list some two months prior from Ms. Carla Del Ponte's assistant. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that was the newspaper publication or the actual printout of the -- from your website is dated the 26th of July, 2006. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that two months prior would have been somewhere around the 26th of May. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. But when I said approximately, that could be mid-May. But on the whole, you are right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, on the Defence response states definitively as the 15th of May. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you also indicated in Exhibit 11 that this assistant of Ms. Del Ponte's was a certain Mr. David Akerson; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you stated so in Exhibit 11. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So how did you know that it came from Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Because all the mail, in the previous case where we were the accused, was always forwarded to the Defence counsel by Mr. Akerson, and since I represented myself, he was the person who sent all the motions and all the materials to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't say because you have received all previous mail from a particular person, therefore a specific document comes from Mr. Akerson, issued -- you are a journalist. You should have proof that it came from Mr. Akerson. How did you know that it came from Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: What I just explained to you was sufficient for me to believe that it was Mr. Akerson who sent me this material, since he was the person who sent all the materials to me in the previous case as the person who represented -- because I represented myself in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you don't say in your -- in your e-mail -- on your website that you believe it's Mr. Akerson. You say it is him. You are definitive.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is what I wrote, because I thought that it was he who sent me that. There was nobody else to send me, because he, on behalf of the Prosecution, disclosed the evidence to the Defence, and there was nobody else to do it. And now Ms. Sutherland is in that role, and in the previous case it was Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you have always received any documentation from Mr. Akerson that he sent to you, because he kept on sending information to you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: With the exception of the first indictment, all the other submissions sent by the Prosecution were signed by Mr. Akerson. And in our case, the indictment was signed by Madam Del Ponte. All the other materials were sent by Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. And you have received it?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did receive this CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you received all other correspondence from Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, apart from the witness list, there were some other documents on this CD that were disclosed to us by the Prosecution in our capacity as Defence counsel. I can't remember what was on there, but I do remember that there was some other material on the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the CD, sir?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Apart from the witness list, I can't remember exactly what else was there. Some other materials pertaining to the previous case before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That CD came via a covering letter, didn't it? Under a covering letter.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. The CD was in a box, in a -- I don't recall which company it was that delivered that, but that CD was in there in that box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there was no covering letter?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. And there was no list detailing everything that I received in the package. The package came, I took receipt of it, and inside was this CD containing the materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you're saying you received a document from a company -- I see a shipment waybill here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The receipt, is that already in evidence, Ms. Sutherland? Yes, under --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2, yes. Perhaps it could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit 2, sir. It's delivered by TNT to you, to Mr. Domagoj Margetic. Do you remember receiving that?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that there were these deliveries coming through TNT all the time, I don't know whether this particular one that you're showing me was one that was actually received by me, but I see there is no signature of mine here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Usually I'd have to sign in a notebook that the delivery man would give me. I had to certify that I received the shipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But according to -- according to the next page, under the same exhibit number, that is [indiscernible - low microphone volume] consignment received in good condition, a Margetic. That's a report from the same company telling us what happened to the delivery.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I am saying to you, Your Honour, that I cannot say whether I did or did not receive this one. I know that my signature's not there, but always I would have to sign for them this very similar piece of paper, very similar to this. I would have to sign it for the delivery man who would make the delivery. Perhaps there were, say, over 30 deliveries that this company brought to me from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The list of witnesses, did you receive it only in CD form? You never received it in hard copy. You talk about three versions of lists that you received. Were they all in CD format?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. All this material was exclusively in CD format. I never received them in any other form. Only on this CD that I got in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those were the questions by Judge Moloto. Does this trigger any questions by the parties? But please keep in mind that we'd like to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but the Prosecution would like to call Mr. Sebastiaan van Hooydonk in rebuttal to ask him a couple of questions. Unless, of course, Your Honours feel that the matter has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that it will deny the request to hear further evidence. Not -- you should not accept this as being based upon what you said if the Chamber thinks the matter has been settled but also, for procedural reasons, there have been opportunities to call other evidence in chief. Mr. Margetic, we have the following in mind: We give you now a couple of minutes to go to the bathroom. Then I'd like to give both parties an opportunity to make a final statement of approximately five minutes, not more, and then also give an opportunity to once add anything in writing if some matter would need some elaboration, and that be filed then on the same day, the Prosecution first and then the Defence. That seems to be a practical arrangement. Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Margetic, you'd take already your time while we are dealing with these procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this suggestion find any objection by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but perhaps five to seven minutes if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are urgent other matters that make it impossible for us. I would say six both and I would be very sharp and strict. Mr. Miljevic, would you oppose the suggested procedure, that is that you have an opportunity, six minutes, to make final argument and then add anything in writing at a time, date, to be set by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it would be useful for the closing argument to be longer. However, as for the key features that I wish to present in defence of my client, I can do that within six minutes' time. However, since I am based in Zagreb, after all, I would kindly ask that the written final submission be made on Monday or Tuesday at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course there's nothing against doing it very quickly, but if we would take more time, then you would have to come back once more, and that seems too much to the Chamber. And since the parties now do agree six minutes each, we will give an opportunity, you, Ms. Sutherland, to be the first one and -- once Mr. Margetic has returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we need to have a break to change the tapes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we don't have to. To be very practical, because it takes more time and we are really having major problems, I now suggest to the parties that final argument would be done in -- totally in writing. These are public documents, so everyone can consult, Mr. Miljevic, because we're really running into trouble if we continue. Would that be agreeable, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When would you want the filing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When do you think you could be ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm on a plane tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that you've written it down anyhow, so in order to present it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We could prepare it -- put it into a filing form this evening and it can be filed on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miljevic, would this be agreeable to you as well? Then you have an opportunity to read first what the Prosecution has written on Monday, and then you have an opportunity, well, let's say another how many time -- how much time would you need, three days, four days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, three or four days after that would suffice for my purposes. On Monday, I'm making my closing arguments in a big trial, 4.500 pages, but if I get this document from the Prosecution on Monday, I will certainly be able to meet the deadline set by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Sutherland, that you will find a way of communicating the document in such a way that Mr. Miljevic has it as soon as possible. Mr. Miljevic, you will then have until the end of next week to file your closing argument in writing. These will be public documents. Mr. Margetic, the Trial Chamber has decided, with the consent of the parties, that final arguments will be made in writing. From the proceedings in this case, I think it has been made abundantly clear where the issues are, so to that extent, there should be no problem to do this in writing, and apart from that, these final arguments in written form are public documents, are available to the parties. Of course the parties should keep in mind that if there is any confidential material dealt with in the final argument, then a redacted version should be provided as well so that it's available to the public. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber adjourns. We'll receive final argument in writing, and of course I couldn't say that for sure at this moment, but most likely, after having received this in due time, the Chamber will give its judgement. We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.
